content.text:
Restatement

We are given a simple undirected graph G with N vertices and M edges. A boomerang is any ordered triple ⟨u, v, w⟩ such that edges (u, v) and (v, w) both exist and u ≠ w. We want to choose as many boomerangs as possible so that each edge of G is used in at most one boomerang (edge-disjoint boomerangs). We can output any maximum set.

Key observations

- A boomerang is completely determined by its center vertex v and two distinct incident edges of v. So the problem is: at as many vertices as possible, pair up incident edges into disjoint pairs; each such pair yields one boomerang centered at that vertex.
- View it as orienting edges towards their “center.” If we decide an edge e = (x, y) is used at center y, think of e as oriented x → y. Then, at vertex v, every pair of incoming edges gives one boomerang centered at v. If indeg(v) is the number of edges oriented into v, then v contributes floor(indeg(v)/2) boomerangs.
- So the optimization is: orient each undirected edge towards one of its endpoints to maximize sum over v of floor(indeg(v)/2). Note that edges we orient but cannot pair simply remain unused; that is okay (we only care that no edge is used more than once).

A linear-time strategy with DFS

We can solve this optimally in O(N + M) using a single DFS traversal plus greedy pairing at each vertex.

The central idea: process the graph in a DFS forest. At each vertex v we collect a bag/list P(v) of “free” incident edges that must be paired at v (that is, if they are to be used at all, v must be their center). We greedily pair edges in P(v) two by two into boomerangs ⟨a, v, b⟩. The only edge that is allowed to “escape” upward out of v is the DFS tree edge to its parent; everything else that touches v is either consumed at v or discarded. This ensures at most one unpaired edge per subtree can try to match outside, which is the best one can hope for across that cut.

What goes into P(v)?

- Non-tree edges (back edges to ancestors): For an undirected DFS, when we see an edge from v to an already visited vertex u (an ancestor), we add this edge to P(v). This edge will never be considered again at u (ensure each edge is processed exactly once), so if it is to be used, it must be centered at v (the deeper endpoint).
- Tree edges from children that were not consumed in the child’s subtree: When we DFS into a child u via e = (v, u), the child may or may not use e locally (to fix odd parity; see below). If the child used e, it’s gone. If not, upon return we add e to P(v), meaning if it is used at all, it will be centered at v.

Parity fix with the parent edge

After P(v) has collected all non-parent edges that must be centered at v, we check its size:

- If v has a parent-edge and |P(v)| is odd, we add the parent-edge to P(v) so that |P(v)| becomes even. Then we can pair all edges in P(v).
- If v is a root (no parent-edge), we simply pair as many as possible: floor(|P(v)|/2) pairs. One edge may remain unpaired in that component; there is no parent-edge to fix parity.

Greedy pairing at v

Once |P(v)| is even (after possibly adding the parent-edge), we repeatedly take any two edges e1 = (v, a) and e2 = (v, b) from P(v) and output one boomerang ⟨a, v, b⟩, marking both edges as used. Because the graph is simple, a ≠ b automatically.

This pairing can be arbitrary; no sophisticated choice is needed.

High-level pseudocode

- Preprocess: store edges with ids and adjacency lists. Maintain:
  - visited[v]: vertex visited in DFS
  - seen[e]: edge already considered once, so it won’t be added twice
  - used[e]: edge already used in some boomerang
  - For output: a list of triples

DFS(v, parent_edge):
  visited[v] = true
  P = empty list (local to v)

  for each incident edge e = (v, u):
    if e == parent_edge: continue
    if not seen[e]:
      seen[e] = true
      if not visited[u]:
        DFS(u, e)
      // After return (or if u was already visited), decide whether to keep e at v
      if not used[e]:
        // this ensures each edge is added exactly once:
        // - back-edges are added at the deeper endpoint v
        // - a child that did not consume its parent edge leaves it for the parent
        P.push(e)

  // Parity fix using the parent edge if possible
  if parent_edge exists and |P| is odd:
    P.push(parent_edge)

  // Pair greedily inside v
  while |P| >= 2:
    e1 = pop(P), e2 = pop(P)
    a = the other endpoint of e1 (≠ v)
    b = the other endpoint of e2 (≠ v)
    output triple (a, v, b)
    used[e1] = used[e2] = true

For all vertices v from 1 to N:
  if not visited[v]:
    DFS(v, no parent)

Why this is correct

1) Every edge is considered exactly once and used at most once.
- We mark an edge e as seen the first time it is encountered during DFS adjacency scans. Only that endpoint (the deeper one for back edges, the parent for a child’s unused tree edge) can add e to some P(·). When we form a boomerang, we mark edges used, and used edges are never added again. Therefore edges are never duplicated across P-bags, and no edge is used twice.

2) Local optimality at a vertex.
- P(v) contains precisely those incident edges that, if used at all, must be centered at v (back edges downwards and child tree edges that bubbled up). If |P(v)| is even we can (and do) use all of them locally. If |P(v)| is odd and v has a parent-edge, consuming the parent-edge at v increases the number of local pairs by 1, which is clearly optimal locally; otherwise (root) one edge must remain unused because there is no other edge left at v to pair with. In all cases, after processing v, no non-parent edge incident to v remains unpaired.

3) Global optimality via cut/induction argument.
- Consider the DFS tree and any subtree T rooted at v. Any boomerang that uses exactly one edge inside T and one outside must involve the unique parent-edge of v, because both edges in a boomerang share a center, hence both are incident to that center; the only way for one edge to be inside T and the other outside is if the center sits at v and one of the edges is the parent-edge. Therefore at most one boomerang can cross the cut between T and the rest of the graph.
- Our procedure ensures the subtree sends upward at most one “need” (it uses the parent-edge if and only if it increases the pair count inside T by 1). By induction on the DFS tree, no algorithm can create more pairs inside T than ours, and no algorithm can beat ours on how many pairs cross the cut (at most one). Summing over the whole forest proves global optimality.

Intuition: everything that can be settled inside a subtree is settled there; only one unresolved edge per subtree (at most) is allowed to try its luck above. Since crossing capacity is at most one per parent-edge, this is optimal.

Complexity

- Each vertex is visited once; each edge is examined O(1) times, pushed into exactly one P(·), and popped at most once. The while-loop across all vertices pairs each used edge exactly once.
- Time: O(N + M)
- Memory: O(N + M) for adjacency, arrays, and the output. This fits 256 MB for M ≤ 1e5.

What to output

- Let K be the number of formed pairs. For each pair e1 = (v, a) and e2 = (v, b) we print the boomerang a v b. Any order of the K boomerangs is acceptable.

Implementation tips

- Give each undirected edge a unique id and store its two endpoints.
- For adjacency, store (neighbor, edge_id) pairs.
- Maintain three boolean arrays of size M: seen[], used[], plus visited[] on vertices.
- The DFS can be iterative to avoid deep recursion if needed.
- When pairing, a and b are the neighbors of v on the chosen edges; in a simple graph they are distinct.

Why it handles all cases

- Disconnected graphs: the outer loop starts a DFS from every unvisited vertex (one leftover edge per component may remain).
- Trees, cycles, general graphs: back edges are always handled at the deeper endpoint; tree edges are used either below (to fix parity) or above (if still unused), ensuring every possible local pairing is realized.
- Sparse and dense graphs: linear-time traversal and per-edge constant work ensure the 0.5 s limit is met.

Summary

- Reduce to: orient each edge to a chosen center to maximize sum of floor indegrees over all vertices, then pair incoming edges at each vertex.
- Solve optimally with a single DFS: collect “must-center-here” edges at each vertex, fix parity using the parent edge, and pair greedily.
- The cut/induction argument shows no solution can pair more edges than this procedure. The algorithm is O(N + M), simple, and yields any valid maximum set of edge-disjoint boomerangs.
